01243ba3 ConvTranspose
01243bb1 xplat/caffe2/caffe2/operators/conv_transpose_op.cc
01243be5 The ConvTranspose op takes an input data tensor $X$, an input weight tensor $filter$, and optionally an input bias tensor $bias$. It then computes the transposed convolution, sometimes referred to as deconvolution, and produces a single output tensor $Y$. The hyperparameters of the op such as kernel size, stride, and padding are specified as args. At each stride, the filter is deconvolved with a subset of $X$ and the $bias$ is added. This is done throughout the input data until the output computation is complete.
01243ded The output shapes are computed as follows. The number of channels in the output feature map is the number of kernels specified in the filter blob. The spatial height and width are computed as:
01243eaf $$H_{out} = (H_{in}-1)*strides[0] - 2*pads[0] + kernels[0]$$
01243eee $$W_{out} = (W_{in}-1)*strides[1] - 2*pads[1] + kernels[1]$$
01243f2c Note on the implementation layout: conv_transpose_op_impl.h is the templated implementation of the conv_transpose_op.h file, which is why they are separate files. Also, in the implementation this operator inherits from the *ConvTransposeUnpoolOpBase* operator.
01244032 Github Links:
01244040 - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/tree/master/caffe2/operators/conv_transpose_op.h
01244096 - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/tree/master/caffe2/operators/conv_transpose_op.cc
012440ed - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/tree/master/caffe2/operators/conv_transpose_unpool_op_base.h

01244f4e Dropout
01244f56 DropoutGrad
01244f64 `Dropout` takes one input data tensor (`X`) and produces two tensor outputs, `Y` and
01244fb9 `mask`. If the `is_test` argument is zero (default=0), the output `Y` will be the input
01245011 with random elements zeroed. The probability that a given element is zeroed is
01245060 determined by the `ratio` argument.
01245085 If the `is_test` argument is set to non-zero, the output `Y` is exactly the same as the
012450dd input `X`. Note that outputs are scaled by a factor of $\frac{1}{1-ratio}$ during
0124512f training, so that during test time, we can simply compute an identity function. This
01245184 scaling is important because we want the output at test time to equal the expected value
012451dd at training time. Dropout has been proven to be an effective regularization technique to
01245236 prevent overfitting during training.
0124525d Github Links:

01246520 xplat/caffe2/caffe2/operators/elu_op.cc
0124654a This op implements the exponential linear unit (ELU) activation function as described in [Fast and Accurate Deep Network Learning by Exponential Linear Units (ELUs)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.07289). The op takes an input tensor $X$ of arbitrary shape, computes the elementwise elu operation, and returns a vector $Y$ of the same shape as output. The alpha parameter may be passed as an argument, but defaults to 1. The elu operation is defined as
0124670c $$y=f(x) =\begin{cases}\alpha(e^x-1) & x < 0 \\ x & otherwise\end{cases}$$

01249cd2 This op fills an output tensor with values sampled from a uniform distribution with the range determined by the desired shape of the output. 0124b60d xplat/caffe2/caffe2/operators/fully_connected_op.cc
0124b642 Same as FC, but weight matrix is supposed to be already pretransposed.
0124b689 FCTransposed stands for calling blass with no noTrans, noTrans
0124b6ca The FC operator computes an output $(Y)$ as a linear combination of the input data blob $(X)$ with a weight blob $(W)$ and bias blob $(b)$. More formally,
0124b766 $$Y = XW^T+b$$
0124b776 Here, $X$ is a matrix of shape $(M,K)$, $W$ is a matrix of shape $(N,K)$, $b$ is a vector of length $N$, and $Y$ is a matrix of shape $(M,N)$. $N$ can be thought of as the number of nodes in the layer, $M$ is the batch size, and $K$ is the number of features in an input observation.
0124b893 *NOTE: $X$ does not need to explicitly be a 2-dimensional matrix, however, if it is not it will be coerced into one. For an arbitrary $n$-dimensional tensor $X$, e.g. $[a_0, a_1, \ldots ,a_{k-1}, a_k, \ldots , a_{n-1}]$, where $a_i$ in $N$, and $k$ is the $axis$ arg provided, then $X$ will be coerced into a 2-dimensional tensor with dimensions $[a_0 * \ldots * a_{k-1}, a_k * \ldots * a_{n-1}]$. For the default case where axis=1, this means the $X$ tensor will be coerced into a 2D tensor of dimensions $[a_0, a_1 * \ldots * a_{n-1}]$, where $a_0$ is often the batch size. In this situation, we must have $a_0 = M$ and $a_1 * \ldots * a_{n-1} = K$. Lastly, even though $b$ is a vector of length $N$, it is copied and resized to shape $(M x N)$ implicitly, then added to each vector in the batch.*
0124bbb4 Github Links:
0124bbc2 - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/caffe2/operators/fully_connected_op.h
0124bc19 - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/caffe2/operators/fully_connected_op.cc

0124d2dc This op fills a uint8 output tensor with the data specified by the *value* argument. The data must previously be serialized as a byte string. 01255164 Softmax
0125516c SoftmaxGradient
0125517c xplat/caffe2/caffe2/operators/softmax_op.cc
012551aa Applies the Softmax function to an n-dimensional input Tensor rescaling them so
012551fa that the elements of the n-dimensional output Tensor lie in the range (0,1) and
0125524a sum to 1. The softmax operator is typically the last layer in a classifier network,
0125529e as its output can be interpreted as confidence probabilities of an input belonging
012552f1 to each class. The input is a 2-D tensor (Tensor) of size (batch_size x
01255339 input_feature_dimensions). The output tensor has the same shape and contains the
0125538a softmax normalized values of the corresponding input. The softmax function is
012553d8 defined as follows:
012553ed $$softmax(x_i) = \frac{\exp(x_i)}{\sum_{j} \exp(x_j)}$$
01255426 The input does not need to explicitly be a 2D vector; rather, it will be coerced
01255477 into one. For an arbitrary n-dimensional tensor `X` in
012554ae $[a_0, a_1, ..., a_{k-1}, a_k, ..., a_{n-1}]$, where k is the `axis` provided,
012554fd then `X` will be coerced into a 2-dimensional tensor with dimensions
01255542 $[(a_0 * ... * a_{k-1}), (a_k * ... * a_{n-1})]$. For the default case where
0125558f `axis`=1, the `X` tensor will be coerced into a 2D tensor of dimensions
012555d7 $[a_0, (a_1 * ... * a_{n-1})]$, where $a_0$ is often the batch size. In this
01255624 situation, we must have $a_0 = N$ and $a_1 * ... * a_{n-1} = D$. Each of these
01255673 dimensions must be matched correctly, or else the operator will throw errors.
012556c2 Github Links:
012556d1 - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/caffe2/operators/softmax_op.h
01255720 - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/caffe2/operators/softmax_op.cc

01256028 SpatialBN
01256032 xplat/caffe2/caffe2/operators/spatial_batch_norm_op.cc
0125606a Applies spatial batch normalization to the input tensor as described in the original paper, [Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03167). Be aware, this operator has two different output sets, depending on the value of *is_test*. According to the paper, the primary operation of spatial batch normalization is:
012561f6 $$Y = \frac{X - \mu_x}{\sqrt{\sigma^2_{x} + \epsilon}}*\gamma + b$$
0125623b In the equation, $\mu_x$ is the *mean*, $X$ is the input data, $\sigma^2_{x}$ is the *var*, $\epsilon$ is *epsilon*, $\gamma$ is the *scale*, $b$ is the *bias*, and $Y$ is the output data. The *momentum* arg also affects this calculation in the computation of the running mean and variance. The influence of *momentum* is as follows:
0125638a $$running\_mean = running\_mean * momentum + mean * (1 - momentum)$$
012563d0 $$running\_var = running\_var * momentum + var * (1 - momentum)$$
01256413 Output when is_test = 0 (train mode): *Y, mean, var, saved_mean, saved_var*
01256460 Output when is_test = 1 (test mode): *Y*
0125648a Github Links:
01256498 - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/caffe2/operators/spatial_batch_norm_op.cc
012564f3 - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/caffe2/operators/spatial_batch_norm_op.h
0125654f *(type: int; default: 0)* If set to nonzero, run spatial batch normalization in test mode.
012565aa momentum
012565b3 *(type: float; default: 0.9)* Factor used in computing the running mean and variance. e.g., running_mean = running_mean x momentum + mean x (1 - momentum)
0125664e num_batches
0125665a *(type: int; default: 1)* Specifies the number of batches to apply normalization on. Requires specifying the optional sums and sumsq inputs that provide statistics across multiple batches from which mean and variance can be determined.
01256746 The input 4-dimensional tensor of shape $NCHW$ or $NHWC$ depending on the order parameter.
012567a1 The scale as a 1-dimensional tensor of size $C$ to be applied to the output.
012567ee The bias as a 1-dimensional tensor of size $C$ to be applied to the output.
0125683a The running mean (training) or the estimated mean (testing) as a 1-dimensional tensor of size $C$.
012568a1 The running variance (training) or the estimated variance (testing) as a 1-dimensional tensor of size $C$.
0125690c sums
01256911 *(optional)* Per-channel sums of elements to be used to determine the mean and variance for this batch.
01256979 sumsq
0125697f *(optional)* Per-channel sum of elements squared per channel to be used to determine the variance for this batch.
012569f1 The output 4-dimensional tensor of the same shape as $X$.
01256a2b The running mean after the spatial BN operator. Must be in-place with the input *mean*. Should not be used for testing.
01256aa3 The running variance after the spatial BN operator. Must be in-place with the input *var*. Should not be used for testing.
01256b1e Saved mean used during training to speed up gradient computation. Should not be used for testing.
01256b80 saved_var
01256b8a Saved variance used during training to speed up gradient computation. Should not be used for testing.

012575b7 to the `axes` argument. Similar to numpy's
012575e2 [transpose](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/numpy/reference/generated/numpy.transpose.html)

01257aa8 Computes the AdaDelta update (https://arxiv.org/abs/1212.5701) for an input
01257af4 gradient and accumulated history of squared gradients. Concretely, given
01257b3d inputs (param, moment, moment_delta, grad, learning_rate), computes:

01257c41     new_moment_delta = moment_delta * decay + square(new_grad) * (1 - decay)

012594b0 xplat/caffe2/caffe2/sgd/adam_op.cc
012594d5 Computes the Adam update (https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6980) for an
01259517 input gradient and momentum parameters. Concretely, given inputs
01259558 (param, m1, m2, grad, lr, iters),
0125957b     t = iters + 1
0125958d     correction_multiplier = sqrt(1 - power(beta2, t)) /
012595c5       (1 - power(beta1, t))
012595e1     m1_o = (beta1 * m1) + (1 - beta1) * grad
0125960e     m2_o = (beta2 * m2) + (1 - beta2) * np.square(grad)
01259646     grad_o = correction_multiplier * m1_o / \
01259674         (sqrt(m2_o) + epsilon)
01259693     param_o = param + lr * grad_o
012596b6 and returns (param_o, m1_o, m2_o, grad_o), in which grad_o is an optional output

0125e033       Learning Rate Adaption is an operation that perform one iteration of
0125e07e       gradient descent based on learning rate:
0125e0ad         lr(k) = lr(k-1) - lr_alpha * df(k-1)/dlr,
0125e0df       where df(k-1)/dlr is the gradient of objective function f on lr, and
0125e12a       lr_alpha is a learning rate hyperparameter. It can be prove that
0125e171       df(k-1)/dlr equals INNERPRODUCT(grad(k-1), -grad(k-2)), where grad(k-1) is
0125e1c2       the grad of f(k-1) on parameters. When the argument
0125e1fc       "normalized_lr_adaption" is false, we simply perform the
0125e23b       following update:
0125e253       lr(k) = lr(k-1) - lr_alpha * INNERPRODUCT(grad(k-1), grad(k-2)).
0125e29a       If we set "normalized_lr_adaption" to be true, we do not directly apply
0125e2e8       INNERPRODUCT(grad(k-1), -grad(k-2)) as the grad. Instead, we perform the
0125e337       following update:
0125e34f       lr(k) = lr(k-1) + lr_alpha * cosineSimilarity(grad(k-1), grad(k-2)).

01266565 xplat/caffe2/caffe2/sgd/storm_op.cc
0126658b Computes the STORM (https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.10018) update for an input
012665d5 gradient and accumulated history of gradients. Concretely, given inputs
0126661d (param, moment, grad_sq_sum, grad, lr), computes:
01266650     new_grad_sq_sum = grad_sq_sum + norm(grad)^2
01266681     effective_lr = lr / (beta + new_grad_sq_sum)^1/3
012666b6     alpha = momentum * square(effective_lr)
012666e2     new_moment = grad + (1 - alpha) * (moment - grad)
01266718     new_param = param + effective_lr * new_moment
0126674b and returns (new_param, new_moment, new_grad_sq_sum).
01266782 Note that due to caffe2 limitation, it is difficult to re-calculate gradient
012667cf in the previous iteration using the current example. We simplied calculation
0126681c for new_moment by using the gradient from the current iteration.

012db383 Scatter takes three inputs `data`, `updates`, and `indices` of the same
012db3cb rank r >= 1 and an optional attribute axis that identifies an axis of `data`
012db418 (by default, the outer-most axis, that is axis 0). The output of the operation
012db467 is produced by creating a copy of the input `data`, and then updating its value
012db4b7 to values specified by `updates` at specific index positions specified by
012db501 `indices`. Its output shape is the same as the shape of `data`.
012db542 For each entry in `updates`, the target index in `data` is obtained by combining
012db593 the corresponding entry in `indices` with the index of the entry itself: the
012db5e0 index-value for dimension = axis is obtained from the value of the corresponding
012db631 entry in `indices` and the index-value for dimension != axis is obtained from the
012db683 index of the entry itself.
012db69f For instance, in a 2-D tensor case, the update corresponding to the [i][j] entry
012db6f0 is performed as below:
012db70b   output[indices[i][j]][j] = updates[i][j] if axis = 0, 
012db744   output[i][indices[i][j]] = updates[i][j] if axis = 1,
012db781 This operator is the inverse of GatherElements. It is similar to Torch's Scatter operation.

012db7ed   data = [
012db7f8       [0.0, 0.0, 0.0],
012db80f       [0.0, 0.0, 0.0],
012db826       [0.0, 0.0, 0.0],
012db841   indices = [
012db84f       [1, 0, 2],
012db860       [0, 2, 1],

012db883       [1.0, 1.1, 1.2],
012db89a       [2.0, 2.1, 2.2],

012db8ee       [0.0, 2.1, 1.2]

012db9a6 ScatterND takes three inputs `data` tensor of rank r >= 1, `indices` tensor of rank q >= 1,
012dba02 and `updates` tensor of rank q + r - indices.shape[-1] - 1. The output of the operation
012dba5a is produced by creating a copy of the input `data`, and then updating its value to values
012dbab4 specified by `updates` at specific index positions specified by `indices`. Its output shape
012dbb10 is the same as the shape of `data`. Note that `indices` should not have duplicate entries.
012dbb6b That is, two or more `updates` for the same index-location is not supported.
012dbbb9 `indices` is an integer tensor. Let k denote indices.shape[-1], the last dimension in the shape of `indices`.
012dbc27  `indices` is treated as a (q-1)-dimensional tensor of k-tuples, where each k-tuple is a partial-index into `data`.
012dbc9b Hence, k can be a value at most the rank of `data`. When k equals rank(data), each update entry specifies an
012dbd08 update to a single element of the tensor. When k is less than rank(data) each update entry specifies an
012dbd70 update to a slice of the tensor.
012dbd92 `updates` is treated as a (q-1)-dimensional tensor of replacement-slice-values. Thus, the
012dbdec first (q-1) dimensions of updates.shape must match the first (q-1) dimensions of indices.shape.
012dbe4c The remaining dimensions of `updates` correspond to the dimensions of the
012dbe96 replacement-slice-values. Each replacement-slice-value is a (r-k) dimensional tensor,
012dbeec corresponding to the trailing (r-k) dimensions of `data`.  Thus, the shape of `updates`
012dbf44 must equal indices.shape[0:q-1] ++ data.shape[k:r-1], where ++ denotes the concatenation
012dbf9d of shapes.
012dbfa9 The `output` is calculated via the following equation:
012dbfe1     output = np.copy(data)
012dbffc     update_indices = indices.shape[:-1]
012dc024     for idx in np.ndindex(update_indices):
012dc04f         output[indices[idx]] = updates[idx]
012dc07c The order of iteration in the above loop is not specified.
012dc0b7 In particular, indices should not have duplicate entries: that is, if idx1 != idx2, then indices[idx1] != indices[idx2].
012dc130 This ensures that the output value does not depend on the iteration order.
012dc17c This operator is the inverse of GatherND.
012dc1a7 Example 1:
012dc1b6   data    = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
012dc1db   indices = [[4], [3], [1], [7]]
012dc1fc   updates = [9, 10, 11, 12]
012dc218   output  = [1, 11, 3, 10, 9, 6, 7, 12]
012dc245 Example 2:
012dc254   data    = [[[1, 2, 3, 4], [5, 6, 7, 8], [8, 7, 6, 5], [4, 3, 2, 1]],
012dc29b              [[1, 2, 3, 4], [5, 6, 7, 8], [8, 7, 6, 5], [4, 3, 2, 1]],
012dc2e2              [[8, 7, 6, 5], [4, 3, 2, 1], [1, 2, 3, 4], [5, 6, 7, 8]],

012dfd28 Given `data` tensor of rank `r` >= 1, `indices` tensor of rank `q` >= 1, and `batch_dims` integer `b`, this operator gathers 
012dfda6 slices of `data` into an output tensor of rank `q + r - indices_shape[-1] - 1 - b`.
012dfdfb `indices` is an q-dimensional integer tensor, best thought of as a `(q-1)`-dimensional tensor of index-tuples into `data`, 
012dfe77 where each element defines a slice of `data`
012dfea5 `batch_dims` (denoted as `b`) is an integer indicating the number of batch dimensions, i.e the leading `b` number of dimensions of 
012dff29 `data` tensor and `indices` are representing the batches, and the gather starts from the `b+1` dimension. 
012dff95 Some salient points about the inputs' rank and shape:
012dffcd 1) r >= 1 and q >= 1 are to be honored. There is no dependency condition to be met between ranks `r` and `q`
012e003b 2) The first `b` dimensions of the shape of `indices` tensor and `data` tensor must be equal.
012e009a 3) b < min(q, r) is to be honored.
012e00be 4) The `indices_shape[-1]` should have a value between 1 (inclusive) and rank `r-b` (inclusive) 
012e0120 5) All values in `indices` are expected to be within bounds [-s, s-1] along axis of size `s` (i.e.) `-data_shape[i] <= indices[...,i] <= data_shape[i] - 1`.
012e01bd    It is an error if any of the index values are out of bounds.
012e01fe The output is computed as follows:
012e0222 The output tensor is obtained by mapping each index-tuple in the `indices` tensor to the corresponding slice of the input `data`.
012e02a6 1) If `indices_shape[-1] > r-b` => error condition
012e02da 2) If `indices_shape[-1] == r-b`, since the rank of `indices` is `q`, `indices` can be thought of as `N` `(q-b-1)`-dimensional tensors
012e0361    containing 1-D tensors of dimension `r-b`, where `N` is an integer equals to the product of 1 and all the elements in the batch dimensions 
012e03f0    of the indices_shape. Let us think of each such `r-b` ranked tensor as `indices_slice`. Each *scalar value* corresponding to `data[0:b-1,indices_slice]` 
012e048d    is filled into the corresponding location of the `(q-b-1)`-dimensional tensor to form the `output` tensor (Example 1 below)
012e050d 3) If `indices_shape[-1] < r-b`, since the rank of `indices` is `q`, `indices` can be thought of as `N` `(q-b-1)`-dimensional tensor
012e0592    containing 1-D tensors of dimension `< r-b`. Let us think of each such tensors as `indices_slice`. Each *tensor slice* corresponding 
012e061b    to `data[0:b-1, indices_slice , :]` is filled into the corresponding location of the `(q-b-1)`-dimensional tensor 
012e0691    to form the `output` tensor (Examples 2, 3, 4 and 5 below)
012e06d0 This operator is the inverse of `ScatterND`.
012e06fe `Example 1`
012e070b   batch_dims = 0
012e071d   data    = [[0,1],[2,3]]   # data_shape = [2, 2]
012e0750   indices = [[0,0],[1,1]]   # indices_shape = [2, 2]
012e0786   output  = [0,3]           # output_shape = [2]
012e07b8 `Example 2`
012e07c5   batch_dims = 0
012e07d7   data    = [[0,1],[2,3]]  # data_shape = [2, 2]

012e0c1f The three supported `modes` are (similar to corresponding modes supported by `numpy.pad`):
012e0c7b 1) `constant`(default) - pads with a given constant value as specified by `constant_value` (which defaults to 0)

012e1131 The UnfoldToDepth operator extracts sliding blocks from an input tensor, and concatenates these blocks
012e1198 in the last dimension.
012e11af Given an input of shape (N x C x D1 x D2 ... x Dn), output would be a 3-D tensor of shape:<br/>
012e1210 ```(N, C * reduce-mul(block_size), reduce-mul(num_blocks))```
012e124e <br/>
012e1254 Where number of blocks extracted from each spatial dimension d is:
012e129b num_blocks[d] = floor((input_spatial_shape[d] + 2 * padding[d] - dilation[d] * (kernel_size[d] - 1) - 1) / stride[d]) + 1
012e131a Input data tensor from previous layer; has size (N x C x H x W), where N is the batch size, C is the number of channels, and H and W are the height and width. Note that this is for the 2D image. Otherwise the size is (N x C x D1 x D2 ... x Dn). 
012e1410 Output data tensor that contains the result of the unfold. The output has three dimensions, and dimension values are funciton of the kernel size, stride size, and pad lengths.
012e14c0 Constrain input and output types to numeric tensors.
012e14f5 The size of the extracted blocks [D1, D2, ..., Dn].
012e1529 Dilation value along each spatial axis of the extracted blocks. If not present, the dilation defaults is 1 along each spatial axis.
012e15ad Stride along each spatial axis of the input image. If not present, the stride defaults is 1 along each spatial axis.
012e1622 Padding for the beginning and ending along each spatial axis, it can take any value greater than or equal to 0. The value represent the number of pixels added to the beginning and end part of the corresponding axis. `pads` format should be as follow [x1_begin, x2_begin...x1_end, x2_end,...], where xi_begin the number of pixels added at the beginning of axis `i` and xi_end, the number of pixels added at the end of axis `i`. If not present, the padding defaults to 0 along start and end of each spatial axis.

01885fd0 NSt6__ndk110__function6__baseIFvRN6caffe28OpSchemaEEEE
01886008 The Conv2D operator computes a 2D convolution operation over an input blob $(X)$, with a filter blob $(filter)$ and a bias blob $(bias)$, and outputs a single output blob $(Y)$. Although there are several options for order, the convention is that the input $(X)$ is a blob of shape $(N,C_{in},H_{in},W_{in})$ and the output $(Y)$ is a blob of shape $(N,C_{out},H_{out},W_{out})$. Here, $N$ is the batch size, $C$ is the number of channels, $H$ is the spatial height, and $W$ is the spatial width. For example, if your input data was a batch of five, 100x120pixel RGB images, $X$ would have shape $(5,3,120,100)$.
0188626e The $filter$ input blob may contain multiple filters and has shape $(M, C_{in}, K_H, K_W)$. Here, $M$ is the number of individual filters contained in the blob, $C_{in}$ is the number of channels of each filter (by convention in 2D convolution it is the same as the number of channels in the input), $K_H$ is the spatial height of the kernel, and $K_W$ is the spatial width of the kernel. The $bias$ blob is a vector of length $M$, where there is one bias for each filter in the $filter$ blob.
0188645d Given the shape of the input blob and the filter blob, we can calculate the shape of the output blob as follows. The number of items in the batch $N$ will stay the same. The number of channels in the output will equal the number of kernels in the filter blob, so $C_{out} = M.$ With stride and pad defined below, the spatial height and width of the output ($H_{out}$ and $W_{out}$) are calculated as
018865ee $$H_{out} = \left \lfloor{\frac{H_{in} - K_H + 2*pad}{stride}+1}\right \rfloor$$
01886641 $$W_{out} = \left \lfloor{\frac{W_{in} - K_W + 2*pad}{stride}+1}\right \rfloor$$
01886694 Github Links:
018866a3 - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/caffe2/operators/conv_op.h
018866ef - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/caffe2/operators/conv_op.cc
0188673c - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/caffe2/operators/conv_pool_op_base.h

01889470 NSt6__ndk110__function6__funcIZN6caffe223AveragePoolDocGeneratorEPKcE3$_0NS_9allocatorIS5_EEFvRNS2_8OpSchemaEEEE
018894e2 consumes an input blob and applies average pooling across the the blob according
01889533 to kernel sizes, stride sizes, pad lengths and dilation. Average pooling consists
01889585 of taking the average value of a subset of the input tensor according to the kernel
018895d9 size and downsampling the data into the output blob for further processing. The
01889629 `brew` module has a wrapper for this operator for use in a `ModelHelper` object.
0188967b Pooling layers reduce the spatial dimensionality of the input blob. Each of the
018896cb output blob's dimensions will reduce according to:
018896ff $$dim_{out}=\frac{dim_{in}-kernel+2*pad}{stride}+1$$

01889d2e kernel sizes, stride sizes, pad lengths and dilation. Max pooling consists of
01889d7c taking the maximum value of a subset of the input tensor according to the kernel
01889dcd size and downsampling the data into the output blob for further processing. The
01889e1d `brew` module has a wrapper for this operator for use in a `ModelHelper` object.
01889e6f Pooling layers reduce the spatial dimensionality of the input blob. Each of the
01889ebf output blob's dimensions will reduce according to:
01889ef3 $$dim_{out}=\frac{dim_{in}-kernel+2*pad}{stride}+1$$
01889f29 Github Links:
01889f38 - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/caffe2/operators/pool_op.h
01889f84 - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/caffe2/operators/pool_op.cc
01889fd1 - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/caffe2/operators/conv_pool_op_base.h
0188a028 <details>

0188a17c print("Y:\n", workspace.FetchBlob("Y"))
